name: Ancient Egypt
blurb: Three thousand years of pharaohs, from Narmer to Alexander
dateConvention: All dates are BC, counting down with no year zero. Egyptian dates before about 690 BC are reconstructions and can be out by decades or more; the deck follows the chronology of Ian Shaw's Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000) throughout and marks every date before 690 BC as approximate. Hatshepsut's card starts when she became regent for the young Thutmose III, and his card covers his sole rule after her death.
epilogue: Alexander was welcomed as pharaoh, visited the oracle at Siwa and founded Alexandria in 331 BC. After his death his general Ptolemy took Egypt, and the Ptolemaic Egypt deck continues the story.

reigns.tagline: The southern king who wore both crowns
reigns.previously: The Nile is split between rival kingdoms in the south and the Delta.
paragraphs: Before Narmer, the Nile valley was a patchwork. In the south, Upper Egypt, rival kingdoms grew up around Nekhen (Hierakonpolis), Naqada and This, near Abydos. In the north lay the marshy Delta, Lower Egypt. Around 3100 BC a southern king called Narmer ruled both halves. Historians start the Early Dynastic Period and the 1st Dynasty with him. Nobody knows how long he reigned, or quite how he pulled it off.

His calling card is the Narmer Palette, a carved siltstone slab found at Hierakonpolis by James Quibell and Frederick Green in their 1897–98 dig, and now in Cairo. On one side he wears the tall white crown of the south and raises a mace over a kneeling enemy. On the other he wears the red crown of the north and marches out to inspect rows of beheaded bodies.

His name, written with a catfish and a chisel, turns up on pots and seals all over Egypt and even in southern Canaan. Later Egyptians said their first king was Menes, founder of Memphis. Narmer may be that man. He was buried in the desert cemetery of Umm el-Qa'ab at Abydos, and the kings who came after him chose the same ground.

claims.text: Narmer is Menes, the legendary first king of Egypt.
claims.note: Menes appears only in king lists written over a thousand years later and in Manetho. Some scholars match him with Narmer, others with his successor Aha.

claims.text: The Narmer Palette records a real war of conquest.
claims.note: It may show a real victory, or a ceremonial picture of what a king was supposed to do. It was a temple offering, not a news report.

claims.text: Menes founded Memphis by damming the Nile, and was later carried off by a hippopotamus.
claims.note: Herodotus tells the dam story; the hippo comes from Manetho as quoted by the chronicler Africanus. Both wrote thousands of years later.

reigns.hook: Narmer's heirs inherit a brand-new kind of country: one king, two crowns, and a court learning to write. The kings of the 1st Dynasty will not go to their graves alone.

reigns.title: The First Dynasty
reigns.tagline: Egypt's first kings, and the servants buried with them
reigns.previously: Narmer rules north and south. Egypt is one kingdom.
paragraphs: After Narmer came Aha, Djer, Djet, Den, Anedjib, Semerkhet and Qaa. One woman stands out among them: Merneith, mother of Den. Her tomb lies among the kings' at Abydos, and she may have ruled for her son while he was young. If so, she was the first woman to run Egypt. Den himself is the first king shown wearing the double crown, the red and white crowns of north and south joined together.

The royal tombs at Umm el-Qa'ab were ringed by rows of small graves for servants and officials. Many of these people seem to have died when the king did, to serve him in the next world. The practice stops after this dynasty. Big mudbrick tombs at Saqqara, near the new city of Memphis, were once taken for the real royal tombs. Most experts now think high officials were buried there.

Meanwhile the state took shape: writing on labels and seals, a calendar, taxes and a court. By the Middle Kingdom, nearly a thousand years on, Egyptians believed Djer's tomb at Abydos was the tomb of the god Osiris himself, and pilgrims left offerings there for centuries. The line ended with Qaa, and what came next is murky.

claims.text: Merneith ruled Egypt as regent for her son Den.
claims.note: Her tomb is royal in scale and a seal from Abydos lists her among the early kings as king's mother. No text says outright that she ruled.

claims.text: Servants and officials were killed to be buried with the king.
claims.note: The rows of graves were dug and roofed together with the royal tomb, which points to sacrifice. No written source describes it.

claims.text: The great Saqqara mastabas were the kings' real tombs.
claims.note: Their excavator Walter Emery thought so. Most Egyptologists now see them as tombs of top officials, with the kings buried at Abydos.

reigns.hook: Qaa's death ends the 1st Dynasty. The next kings leave little behind but a puzzle: why would one of them swap the falcon god Horus for Seth, god of chaos?

reigns.title: The Second Dynasty
reigns.tagline: A dark age, a rebel god, and a king who fixed it
reigns.cameToPower: Unclear; a new family takes over
reigns.previously: Qaa dies and the 1st Dynasty comes to an end.
paragraphs: The 2nd Dynasty is one of the darkest corners of Egyptian history. We have names, Hetepsekhemwy, Raneb (also read Nebra), Nynetjer and others, but little about what they did. Then something odd happened. King Peribsen put the god Seth on top of his name, in the spot where kings always showed the falcon Horus.

That could mean a religious shake-up, a split kingdom or even civil war. Order came back under Khasekhemwy, whose name means "the two powers appear". Above it sat both Horus and Seth, side by side. Statue bases from Hierakonpolis boast of vast numbers of northern enemies killed. He may be the same man as a king called Khasekhem, who changed his name once the fighting was won.

Khasekhemwy built big. His giant mudbrick enclosure at Abydos, the Shunet el-Zebib, still stands after nearly 5,000 years. Later Egyptians honoured a royal woman of his time, Nimaathap, as the ancestress of the next royal house. That family was about to switch from mud to stone.

claims.text: Peribsen's Seth name shows Egypt was split by civil war.
claims.note: The Seth name is real. What it meant is guesswork: a religious change, a rival northern or southern king, or a rebel.

claims.text: Khasekhem and Khasekhemwy were one king who renamed himself.
claims.note: The two names never appear together, and their monuments are similar. Many scholars think it was one man; some think two.

claims.text: Khasekhemwy killed huge numbers of northerners.
claims.note: The numbers come from royal statue bases, boasts carved to impress, which cannot be checked.

reigns.hook: Khasekhemwy's mudbrick walls are the last word in royal building. Within a generation, a king and his clever official will build a mountain out of cut stone.

images.caption: A seated statue of the king from Hierakonpolis, inscribed with the name Khasekhem; Egyptian royal statues show an ideal, not a true likeness.
images.alt: Ancient stone seated statue of King Khasekhemwy, wrapped in a robe, from Hierakonpolis

reigns.tagline: The first pyramid, and the genius who designed it
reigns.reignEnded: Died; buried at the Step Pyramid
reigns.previously: Khasekhemwy reunites Egypt. A new dynasty takes the throne.
paragraphs: In his own day he was called Netjerikhet. The name Djoser only turns up in records written long afterwards. The dates used here put a king called Nebka just before him, though many Egyptologists now think Djoser came first. Either way, his reign belongs to the start of the Old Kingdom, the age of the pyramids, and he kicked it off with something nobody had ever seen.

At Saqqara, high above Memphis, rose the Step Pyramid: six stacked stages of stone, over 60 metres tall, at the heart of a vast walled complex of courts, shrines and dummy buildings. It is often called the first monumental building made entirely of cut stone. The designer was his official Imhotep, whose name and titles are carved on the base of a statue of the king.

Imhotep's fame outlived his master's. About 2,000 years later Egyptians worshipped him as a god of healing and wisdom, and the Greeks matched him with their medicine god, Asclepius. Djoser still keeps watch too. His painted limestone statue was found sealed in a tiny room beside the pyramid, peering out through two eye-holes. The original is in Cairo; a copy sits in its place.

claims.text: The Step Pyramid is the first monumental building made entirely of cut stone.
claims.note: Earlier kings used some stone, including in Khasekhemwy's tomb, but nothing on this scale is known before it.

claims.text: Djoser ended a seven-year famine by honouring the god Khnum.
claims.note: The Famine Stela on Sehel Island tells the story, but it was carved under the Ptolemies, over 2,000 years later, probably to back the claims of Khnum's priests.

claims.text: Djoser came before Nebka, not after him.
claims.note: Shaw puts Nebka first. Seal impressions naming Netjerikhet in Khasekhemwy's tomb lead many scholars to put Djoser right after Khasekhemwy.

reigns.hook: Djoser has shown what stone can do. Two generations on, a new king will try to go bigger, and his first attempts will not all go to plan.

reigns.tagline: Three pyramids, one wobble, and a king people liked
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Successor of Huni; perhaps his son
reigns.previously: Djoser's heirs can't match his pyramid. Huni ends the 3rd Dynasty.
paragraphs: Sneferu founded the 4th Dynasty and probably shifted more stone than any other pharaoh. First came Meidum, a step pyramid that his predecessor Huni may have begun. Then, at Dahshur, the Bent Pyramid, which starts steep and switches to a gentler slope halfway up. Maybe the builders saw cracks and lost their nerve. Maybe they were in a hurry. Nobody knows for sure.

His third attempt worked. The Red Pyramid, also at Dahshur, was the first true pyramid with smooth, straight sides, and he was probably buried in it. Egypt's armies were busy too. The Palermo Stone, a slab of royal annals, records raids into Nubia and Libya that brought home captives and herds of cattle.

Later Egyptians remembered Sneferu as a kind, easy-going king who chatted with his courtiers as friends. With his queen, Hetepheres I, he had a son: Khufu. In 1925 George Reisner's team found her reburied tomb goods at Giza, gilded furniture and all, at the bottom of a deep shaft beside her son's pyramid.

claims.text: Bored at court, Sneferu was rowed round his lake by twenty girls dressed in fishing nets; when one dropped her turquoise pendant, a magician folded back the water to fetch it.
claims.note: From the Westcar Papyrus, a collection of tales written down centuries after Sneferu's death.

claims.text: The Bent Pyramid changed angle because it started to crack.
claims.note: Cracks and repairs inside are real. Whether they caused the change, or the builders just wanted to finish faster, is argued.

claims.text: Sneferu moved more stone than any other pharaoh.
claims.note: Add up Meidum, the Bent and the Red Pyramids and he beats even Khufu, but the totals are estimates and Meidum may be partly Huni's.

reigns.hook: Sneferu dies remembered for his kindness. His son Khufu will be remembered very differently, and he wants the biggest pyramid of all.

reigns.tagline: The biggest pyramid ever, and a statue you could hide
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Sneferu and Hetepheres I
reigns.reignEnded: Died; buried in the Great Pyramid
reigns.previously: Sneferu builds three pyramids and dies a much-loved king.
paragraphs: The Greeks called him Cheops. His Great Pyramid at Giza is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing. It took more than two million blocks of stone and roughly two decades of work by skilled crews, labourers and boatmen. When finished it stood about 146 metres high.

We even know a few of the workers. In 2013 Pierre Tallet's team found papyri at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea coast: the logbook of an inspector named Merer. His crew shipped fine limestone from the quarries at Tura, across the river, to Giza for the pyramid's casing. They are the oldest inscribed papyri ever found. In 1954 a full-size cedar boat turned up, taken apart and sealed in a pit beside the pyramid.

For all that, the only certain statue of Khufu is a little ivory figure about 7.5 cm tall, found by Flinders Petrie's team at Abydos in 1903. Greek visitors 2,000 years later heard dark stories about him. Herodotus was told that Cheops was a tyrant who shut the temples and worked his people to exhaustion. Two of his sons would wear the crown after him.

claims.text: Cheops was so short of money that he put his own daughter to work in a brothel.
claims.note: Herodotus heard it from guides about 2,000 years after Khufu. Nothing from Khufu's own time hints at it.

claims.text: The Great Pyramid was the tallest man-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years.
claims.note: It is usually said to have been overtaken by Lincoln Cathedral's spire in the early 14th century, but both heights are estimates.

claims.text: Merer's diary records stone being shipped for the Great Pyramid.
claims.note: The papyri date to late in Khufu's reign and were published by Tallet. They are the earliest eyewitness account of pyramid building.

reigns.hook: Khufu lies in the biggest tomb on Earth. His sons now face an awkward question: how do you follow that?

reigns.tagline: The pyramid that looks taller, and maybe the Sphinx
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Khufu; brother of Djedefre
reigns.previously: Khufu's son Djedefre reigns briefly, starting a pyramid at Abu Rawash.
paragraphs: Khufu's son Djedefre reigned only from 2566 to 2558 BC and began a pyramid at Abu Rawash, north of Giza. Then another son of Khufu took over: Khafre, whom the Greeks called Chephren. He went back to Giza and built right next to his father.

His pyramid is a little smaller than Khufu's but looks taller, because it stands on higher ground. Near the top it still wears a cap of the smooth casing stones that once covered the whole thing. Below it crouches the Great Sphinx, a lion with a king's head, carved out of the bedrock. It is usually credited to Khafre.

His finest portrait is a seated statue in dark gneiss. The falcon god Horus perches behind the king's head and spreads its wings around it, as if on guard. Auguste Mariette found it in 1860 in a pit in Khafre's valley temple. It is now one of the great treasures of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

claims.text: Khafre had the Great Sphinx carved.
claims.note: It lines up with his valley temple and causeway, and the face may be his, but no ancient inscription names its maker.

claims.text: The Egyptians hated Cheops and Chephren so much they would not speak their names, and called the pyramids after a shepherd.
claims.note: Herodotus heard this from his guides about 2,000 years later. Both kings were honoured by cults for centuries.

reigns.hook: Khafre's pyramid towers over Giza. The next king will build a much smaller one, and the Greeks will remember him as the good man among tyrants.

reigns.tagline: The smallest Giza pyramid, the finest statues
reigns.previously: Khafre builds the second pyramid at Giza, and maybe the Sphinx.
paragraphs: The Greeks called him Mycerinus. His pyramid is the smallest of the big three at Giza, less than half the height of Khufu's. What his reign lacked in size it made up for in style. Between 1908 and 1910 George Reisner's Harvard–Boston team dug out his valley temple and found some of the finest statues Egypt ever produced.

There were triads, each showing the king with the goddess Hathor and a local god, and a pair statue of the king standing beside a queen with her arm around his waist. They are carved in greywacke, a hard dark stone, and are now in Boston and Cairo. Herodotus heard that Mycerinus was a fair-minded king who reopened the temples his father and uncle had shut.

After him came Shepseskaf, from 2503 to 2498 BC, the last king of the 4th Dynasty. He broke the pyramid habit and built himself a giant stone tomb shaped like a sarcophagus, the Mastabat Faraun, at Saqqara. The age of the great Giza pyramids was over.

claims.text: An oracle gave Mycerinus six years to live, so he lit lamps every night to turn night into day and live twelve.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, about 2,000 years later, from what priests told him.

claims.text: The queen in the pair statue is Khamerernebty II.
claims.note: No name is carved on the statue. She is the most likely candidate, but it is an educated guess.

claims.text: Menkaure's sarcophagus sank with the ship Beatrice off Spain.
claims.note: Howard Vyse's men removed it from the pyramid in 1837 and sent it to England. The merchant ship Beatrice was lost in 1838 after leaving Malta; where it sank is uncertain and the wreck has never been found.

reigns.hook: Shepseskaf's dynasty fizzles out. The next kings will build smaller pyramids and pour their energy into a new obsession: the sun god Ra.

reigns.title: The Sun Kings
reigns.tagline: Sun temples, smaller pyramids and the first spells in stone
reigns.previously: Shepseskaf, last of the Giza dynasty, is buried in a giant stone tomb.
paragraphs: From Userkaf to Unas, the kings of the 5th Dynasty, among them Sahure, Neferirkare, Nyuserre and Djedkare Isesi, raised the sun god Ra to the top. As well as pyramids at Abusir and Saqqara, far smaller than Giza's, several built sun temples: open courts around a great squat obelisk. Nyuserre's, at Abu Ghurab, is the best preserved.

Their pyramids may be modest, but their paperwork survives. The Abusir papyri, the accounts of Neferirkare's pyramid temple, record duty rosters, offerings and repairs: the daily running of a dead king's cult. Abroad, Sahure's reign is linked with an expedition to Punt, the far-off land of incense and myrrh.

The last king, Unas, made history inside his pyramid at Saqqara. Its burial chambers are covered with the Pyramid Texts, the first time these spells were carved on a pyramid's walls. They are meant to lift the dead king to the sky. In one, now called the "Cannibal Hymn", the king hunts down the gods and eats them to take their power.

claims.text: The first three kings of the dynasty were triplets, fathered by Ra on a priest's wife named Rudjedet.
claims.note: From the Westcar Papyrus, a set of tales written down long afterwards to explain why these kings were so devoted to Ra.

claims.text: Sahure sent an expedition to Punt.
claims.note: The Palermo Stone lists goods from Punt in his reign. Whether his own ships made the trip is less certain.

claims.text: Unas's pyramid has the Cannibal Hymn on its walls.
claims.note: The spell is carved in his burial chambers and repeated in Teti's pyramid. It is translated in the standard editions.

reigns.hook: Unas leaves no son to follow him. The new 6th Dynasty will face something worse than rivals: enemies inside the palace.

reigns.title: Teti, Pepi I and the Harem Plot
reigns.tagline: A murdered king and a secret trial in the harem
reigns.previously: Unas dies, his pyramid covered in spells, with no son to follow him.
paragraphs: Teti founded the 6th Dynasty. Manetho says he was murdered by his own bodyguards. After him comes a shadowy figure, Userkare, who may have been a usurper. Then Teti's son Pepi I took over and reigned for about 34 years, long enough to put his name on temples up and down Egypt.

Our best eyewitness is Weni, an official who wrote his life story in his tomb at Abydos. He says he alone was trusted to hear a secret case against a queen in the royal harem. He never says what she did. Weni also led armies against the "sand-dwellers" north-east of Egypt, and bragged that his troops came home safe after flattening their strongholds and cutting down their figs and vines.

Pepi I was also cast in metal. Two copper statues, a life-size king and a smaller figure, were found at Hierakonpolis in 1897–98. Then came his son Merenre, who reigned from 2287 to 2278 BC. His reign was short, and the crown passed to a small boy.

claims.text: Teti was murdered by his own bodyguards.
claims.note: Only Manetho says so, about 2,000 years later. No text from the Old Kingdom mentions it.

claims.text: Weni secretly heard a case against a queen in the harem.
claims.note: It is in his own tomb inscription, now in Cairo. What the queen did and what became of her are never stated.

claims.text: The copper statues of Pepi I are among the oldest large metal statues known.
claims.note: Few metal statues this early survive, so the claim is likely but hard to prove.

reigns.hook: Merenre is dead. The new king of Egypt is a little boy, and he may be about to reign longer than anyone in history.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who wanted a dancer more than gold
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Probably a son of Pepi I
reigns.previously: Merenre dies after a short reign. The heir is a small boy.
paragraphs: Pepi II came to the throne as a child, with his mother, Ankhnesmeryre II, close beside him. A little alabaster statue in the Brooklyn Museum shows him as a miniature king sitting on her lap. Manetho says he was six when he was crowned and reigned for 94 years.

The best story from his reign is a letter he wrote as a boy, which the expedition leader Harkhuf proudly carved on his tomb at Aswan. Harkhuf had sent word from the land of Yam, far to the south, that he was bringing home a dancing pygmy. The young king could barely contain himself. He wanted to see the dancer more than all the treasures of Sinai and Punt.

He ordered trusty men to sleep beside the dancer on the boat and check on him ten times a night, so he could not fall into the river. Over Pepi's long reign, though, the provincial governors grew rich and built grand tombs at home, acting more like local princes than royal servants. When the old king finally died, the Old Kingdom was running out of road.

claims.text: Pepi II reigned for 94 years, the longest reign in history.
claims.note: Manetho says so and the Turin king list also gives him over 90 years, but some Egyptologists think the dates from his reign point to about 64.

claims.text: The boy king's letter to Harkhuf is genuine.
claims.note: Harkhuf had it carved on the front of his tomb at Qubbet el-Hawa, Aswan, where it can still be read.

claims.text: Powerful provincial governors brought down the Old Kingdom.
claims.note: Their growing wealth is clear from their tombs. How much it caused the collapse, against low floods or a weak succession, is argued.

reigns.hook: Pepi II is dead and his heirs are short-lived. The Old Kingdom falls apart, and Egypt splits between rival kings, hungry provinces and a vengeful queen.

reigns.title: The First Intermediate Period
reigns.tagline: Seventy kings in seventy days, and a hungry south
reigns.previously: Pepi II dies after a record reign, and the old order starts to crack.
paragraphs: Pepi II had reigned so long that hardly anyone alive remembered another king. When he died, the machine he left behind seized up. Kings of the 8th Dynasty hung on at Memphis for a few decades, but they counted for little outside it. Out in the provinces the governors were already little kings, with their own soldiers, their own granaries and their own grand tombs. This is the First Intermediate Period, and for over a century Egypt had no single master.

The Nile made things worse. Low floods meant thin harvests, and the governors' tombs are full of talk of hunger. Ankhtifi of Mo'alla boasts that the whole south was starving, with people eating their own children, while his province alone was fed. By about 2160 BC two royal houses had emerged. Kings at Herakleopolis, south of Memphis, held the north as the 9th and 10th Dynasties. At Thebes a family of kings called Intef built a rival kingdom in the south.

The two sides fought for generations over the land around Abydos. One Herakleopolitan king left a book of advice for his son Merikare, and in it he admits that holy ground near Abydos was wrecked on his watch, and says he regrets it. In the south, Intef II reigned for about 50 years and pushed his border north. Then Intef III's son came to the throne at Thebes, a man named Mentuhotep, who meant to finish the job.

claims.text: Queen Nitocris avenged her murdered brother by drowning his killers at a banquet in a secret underground hall, then threw herself into a room full of ashes.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, some 1,700 years later. A name once read as Nitocris in the Turin king list now looks like a misreading, so she may never have existed.

claims.text: The 7th Dynasty was seventy kings who reigned for seventy days.
claims.note: This comes from Manetho, as quoted by Africanus. It is probably a garbled memory of many short, weak reigns, not a real count.

claims.text: Egypt was gripped by famine caused by failing Nile floods.
claims.note: Governors like Ankhtifi describe starvation, but boasting of feeding the hungry was a stock way to praise yourself. How far climate caused the collapse is still argued.

reigns.hook: Mentuhotep of Thebes has inherited a war that has dragged on for generations. He means to end it, and to make the whole Nile answer to one king again.

reigns.tagline: The Theban who glued Egypt back together
reigns.previously: Egypt is split: Herakleopolis holds the north, Thebes the south.
paragraphs: Mentuhotep II began as one of two kings. His Thebans held the south and the kings of Herakleopolis held the north, and the old war over the middle of the country flared up again. Some time before his 39th year he broke through. Herakleopolis fell, the north submitted, and for the first time in over a century one pharaoh ruled from the Delta to Aswan. He took a new name meaning 'he who unites the Two Lands'. This is the start of the Middle Kingdom.

Then he built. Across the river from Thebes, at Deir el-Bahri, he raised a terraced tomb-temple against the cliffs, unlike anything before it. Nearby lay a tomb packed with about 60 soldiers, many with arrow wounds, killed in some battle and buried with honour. Later Egyptians never forgot him. Their king lists and temple scenes set him beside Menes and Ahmose as one of the great founders of Egypt.

Howard Carter's horse, the story goes, stumbled into a hole in front of the temple. When he dug there in 1900, he found a hidden shaft and a painted sandstone statue of the king, black-skinned, in a white robe and the red crown. Mentuhotep reigned about 51 years. His son Mentuhotep III carried on, but under Mentuhotep IV the family line ran dry, and a vizier named Amenemhat was waiting in the wings.

claims.text: Howard Carter found the hidden statue when his horse stumbled into a hole.
claims.note: Carter's own story, and the reason the spot is called Bab el-Hosan, 'Gate of the Horse'. Nobody else saw it happen.

claims.text: He reunited Egypt around his 39th year.
claims.note: The date is pieced together from changes in his royal names. When and how the war with Herakleopolis ended is not recorded.

claims.text: The 60 soldiers in the nearby tomb died in his war with Herakleopolis.
claims.note: Herbert Winlock, who found them in the 1920s, thought so. Others link them to a different campaign, and some date the burial later.

reigns.hook: Mentuhotep's line is fading out. His last heir sends a vizier named Amenemhat into the desert to fetch a stone coffin, and the vizier comes back with a story about a gazelle.

reigns.tagline: The vizier who became king, and died in the dark
reigns.previously: Mentuhotep II reunites Egypt, but his line soon fades out.
paragraphs: Under Mentuhotep IV, a vizier named Amenemhat led a quarrying expedition into the Wadi Hammamat to fetch a block for the king's sarcophagus. The inscriptions his men carved there report a wonder: a pregnant gazelle walked up to the chosen block and gave birth on it. A good omen, clearly. The question was for whom. Within a few years Mentuhotep IV had vanished from the record, and a king called Amenemhat was founding the 12th Dynasty.

A new man needed a good story, and his scribes wrote one. The Prophecy of Neferti, set back in the days of Sneferu, foretells an age of chaos ended by a saviour king called Ameny, son of a woman from the south. Everyone knew who that meant. Amenemhat moved the capital north from Thebes to a new city, Itjtawy, near Lisht, and built his pyramid there.

After about 30 years it ended at night. A later text puts words in the dead king's mouth, telling his son how armed men came for him after supper while he rested, and no one came to his aid. His son Senusret was away fighting in Libya. Whether the attackers had won, and who would hold the throne, was suddenly up for grabs.

claims.text: Amenemhat was murdered in a palace plot.
claims.note: The Instruction of Amenemhat has his ghost describe the attack, but it was written as political literature in his son's reign. Most Egyptologists think he really was killed.

claims.text: The vizier Amenemhat of the gazelle inscriptions is the same man as King Amenemhat I.
claims.note: The name and timing fit, and most historians accept it, but no text says so outright.

claims.text: Senusret I was already ruling beside his father as co-king.
claims.note: Some monuments carry dates in both reigns, which once suggested a ten-year co-regency. Many scholars now doubt it.

reigns.hook: In the Libyan desert, a messenger reaches the crown prince Senusret with news of his father's death. He tells no one, and slips away for home.

reigns.tagline: He raced home from a murder and ruled for 45 years
reigns.cameToPower: Rushed home on his father's death
reigns.previously: Amenemhat I is attacked in his palace at night.
paragraphs: Our best picture of how he took power comes from a story. The Tale of Sinuhe opens with Senusret leading his army home from Libya when messengers bring word that the old king is dead. He sets off at once, quietly, with only his own men. A courtier called Sinuhe overhears and panics so badly that he flees to Canaan, where he lives for decades as a desert chief before coming home as an old man to beg the king's pardon.

Whatever happened that night, Senusret held on, and reigned about 45 years. He pushed south into Lower Nubia and built forts such as Buhen near the second cataract to guard the routes to the gold mines. He built temples all over Egypt. At Heliopolis one of his obelisks still stands. At Karnak his elegant White Chapel was later pulled down and used as rubble inside a pylon, and in the 20th century it was rebuilt from its original blocks.

The Greeks later remembered kings of his name as Sesostris. Senusret died around 1911 BC, leaving a rich, settled kingdom to his son Amenemhat II. The 12th Dynasty had survived its bloody start and was set to rule for another century and a half.

claims.text: Senusret secretly rushed home from Libya when his father was murdered.
claims.note: This comes from the Tale of Sinuhe, a work of literature, though it is set in real events and real places.

claims.text: His obelisk at Heliopolis is the oldest standing obelisk in Egypt.
claims.note: It is often called that, and it still stands in place in Cairo's Matariya district, but older, broken obelisks are known.

claims.text: He conquered Lower Nubia as far as the second cataract.
claims.note: A stela from Buhen records a campaign in his 18th year, but how far earlier kings had already pushed is debated.

reigns.hook: Two more kings pass in peace. Then Senusret III comes to the throne, a hard soldier with his eyes fixed on Nubia.

reigns.tagline: The careworn warrior who walled off the Nile
reigns.previously: Senusret I dies. Amenemhat II and Senusret II keep the peace.
paragraphs: Senusret III went to Nubia, and kept going back. His boats couldn't get easily past the rocks of the first cataract at Aswan, so he had a channel cut through them. Then he marched south, campaigning year after year, and built a chain of huge mudbrick forts around the second cataract, with thick walls, ditches and lookout posts, to control everything that moved on the river.

At Semna he set up a boundary stela with a blunt message for his heirs. Any son of his who held this border was truly his son. Any who gave it up was no son of his at all. The Nubians remembered him too: centuries later Thutmose III built a temple at Semna where Senusret was worshipped as a god. At home he seems to have cut the great provincial governors down to size.

His statues are unforgettable: a drawn, heavy-lidded face, lined with care, and big ears. Is it a true likeness, an old king's burden, or a message about a ruler who never sleeps? People still argue. The Greeks may have turned him into Sesostris, a hero who conquered the world. His son Amenemhat III inherited a safe, rich kingdom.

claims.text: Senusret III cut the power of the provincial governors.
claims.note: Their great provincial tombs stop being built around his reign. Whether he crushed them or simply drew their sons to court is unclear.

claims.text: His careworn statues were meant to show a king worn down by his duties.
claims.note: That's one reading. Others see a deliberate image of a watchful, all-knowing ruler, or simply a new court style.

claims.text: Sesostris, the hero Herodotus says conquered Asia and Europe, was really Senusret III.
claims.note: Herodotus's Sesostris is a blend of several kings and pure fiction. Senusret III is probably the main model, but he never campaigned beyond Nubia and Canaan.

reigns.hook: The borders are safe and the mines are open. Amenemhat III is about to preside over the richest years the Middle Kingdom ever saw.

reigns.tagline: Golden years, a sinking pyramid and a Labyrinth
reigns.previously: Senusret III dies with Nubia held by a wall of forts.
paragraphs: Amenemhat III had the luck to inherit peace, and he used it. He reigned about 45 years and Egypt was rich. His expeditions worked the turquoise and copper mines of Sinai harder than ever before. He poured effort into the Faiyum, the great lake basin west of the Nile, where swamp was turned into farmland. People there were still worshipping him as a god well over a thousand years later.

He built two pyramids. The first, at Dahshur, is called the Black Pyramid for its dark, crumbling core. It stood on soft ground and began to crack and sink, so he seems to have been buried in his second pyramid, at Hawara in the Faiyum. Beside it stood a vast temple with so many rooms and courts that Greek visitors called it the Labyrinth. Herodotus said it outdid even the pyramids.

His statues are among the most striking in Egypt. The Tanis sphinxes give him a lion's body and a great mane framing a hard, lined face. They were so unusual that scholars once took them for Hyksos work. After him Amenemhat IV reigned about nine years and left no son. The great family was down to its last royal woman.

claims.text: The Labyrinth had 3,000 rooms, half of them underground.
claims.note: Herodotus says so. He claims he toured the upper rooms but was refused entry to the lower ones, said to hold the tombs of kings and sacred crocodiles.

claims.text: He gave up the Black Pyramid because it was sinking and cracking.
claims.note: The damage is real and he probably lay at Hawara, but the Dahshur pyramid was still used for royal women's burials.

claims.text: The Tanis sphinxes were once thought to be portraits of Hyksos kings.
claims.note: Early Egyptologists, misled by later kings' names carved on them, credited them to the Hyksos. Their faces are now recognised as Amenemhat III's.

reigns.hook: Amenemhat IV dies with no son to follow him. For the first time we can be sure of, a woman is about to take the throne of Egypt as king.

reigns.tagline: The first woman we know for sure ruled Egypt as king
reigns.previously: Amenemhat IV dies after about nine years, leaving no son.
paragraphs: Her name means 'beauty of Sobek', after the crocodile god of the Faiyum, and she was probably a daughter of Amenemhat III. When Amenemhat IV died without a son, she took the throne herself. Other women may have ruled Egypt before her, but she is the first we can say for certain ruled as king in her own right, with the full set of royal names.

She made no secret of being a woman, or of being king. A headless statue in the Louvre shows her in a woman's dress, with a king's kilt over it and a royal headcloth falling to her shoulders. Her titles mix female grammar with kingly roles. She added to the great temple at Hawara, honouring Amenemhat III, the father who had made her world.

Her reign was short. The Turin king list, written down centuries later, gives her just under four years. How it ended, nobody knows, and no tomb has been found that is certainly hers. With her, the 12th Dynasty, a family that had held Egypt for about two centuries, came to an end.

claims.text: Sobekneferu was the first woman to rule Egypt as king.
claims.note: She is the first certain one. Merneith of the 1st Dynasty may have ruled as regent, and Nitocris may be a misreading or a legend.

claims.text: The Turin king list gives her a reign of 3 years, 10 months and 24 days.
claims.note: The papyrus does say so, but it was copied about 500 years later and is badly damaged in places.

claims.text: She was buried in one of the two pyramids at Mazghuna, near Dahshur.
claims.note: Some scholars have suggested the northern Mazghuna pyramid, but nothing found there names her.

reigns.hook: Sobekneferu is gone, and the great family with her. Next comes a dynasty of dozens of kings, most of whom barely have time to unpack.

reigns.title: The Thirteenth Dynasty
reigns.tagline: Fifty-odd kings, and the civil service kept going
reigns.previously: Sobekneferu, Egypt's first sure woman king, ends the 12th Dynasty.
paragraphs: Picture a throne with a revolving door. In about 120 years the 13th Dynasty ran through 50 kings or more, many lasting only a year or two. Several were called Sobekhotep, after the crocodile god. Some were plainly not sons of kings at all. It sounds like chaos, but the country kept working. The viziers and officials stayed at their desks in Itjtawy while kings came and went above them, and the Middle Kingdom limped on.

A few kings stand out. Neferhotep I and his brother Sobekhotep IV ruled long enough to leave monuments up and down the Nile. At Dahshur in 1894 the French archaeologist Jacques de Morgan found the burial of a king named Awibre Hor, with a wooden statue of his ka, his life force. On its head sit two raised arms, the hieroglyph for 'ka'.

Meanwhile, in the eastern Delta, the town of Avaris was filling up with people from Canaan: traders, soldiers and craftsmen. They kept their own customs and buried their dead their own way. A rival line of kings, the 14th Dynasty, seems to have ruled from there. Slowly the north slipped from the 13th Dynasty's grip, and the newcomers were about to take charge.

claims.text: The 13th Dynasty had more than 50 kings in about 120 years.
claims.note: The Turin king list names many of them, but it is damaged, and the exact count and order are argued over.

claims.text: A rival 14th Dynasty ruled the eastern Delta from Avaris.
claims.note: Manetho lists one, and seals name kings like Nehesy, but where they ruled and when is uncertain.

reigns.hook: In the Delta, foreign kings are settling in at Avaris. The Egyptians have a name for them, rulers of foreign lands. History will call them the Hyksos.

reigns.title: The Hyksos
reigns.tagline: The foreign kings who ruled Egypt from Avaris
reigns.previously: Kings come and go fast, and settlers from Canaan fill Avaris.
paragraphs: Their name comes from the Egyptian heqau khasut, 'rulers of foreign lands'. They were West Semitic people from Canaan, and by about 1650 BC their kings, the 15th Dynasty, ruled the north from Avaris in the eastern Delta. The best known are Khyan and Apepi. This is the Second Intermediate Period: Egypt split again, with foreigners in the north and a line of Theban kings in the south.

Later Egyptians told it as a horror story. Manetho, writing well over a thousand years later and quoted by Josephus, describes a sudden invasion that burned cities and wrecked temples. The ground tells a quieter tale. Manfred Bietak's digs at Avaris, today's Tell el-Dab'a, show a Canaanite town growing over generations, with its own houses, temples and graves, some with donkeys buried at the tomb door.

The Hyksos were no wreckers. They used Egyptian titles and had Egyptian texts copied: the famous Rhind Mathematical Papyrus was written out in Apepi's 33rd year. Horses and chariots spread in Egypt in their time. Down in the south the Theban kings of the 17th Dynasty ruled their own strip of the Nile, uneasily, and waited.

claims.text: The Hyksos swept into Egypt in a savage invasion, burning cities as they came.
claims.note: That's Manetho, quoted by Josephus. Excavation at Avaris points instead to settlers already living there gradually taking power.

claims.text: The Hyksos were the Israelites of the Bible's Joseph and Exodus stories.
claims.note: Josephus made the link in the 1st century AD to prove the antiquity of the Jews. No evidence connects the two.

claims.text: The Hyksos brought the horse and chariot to Egypt.
claims.note: Both appear in Egypt around this time, but how much the Hyksos had to do with it is debated.

reigns.hook: Apepi sits at Avaris. Far to the south, the Theban king Seqenenre is about to receive a very strange complaint about some noisy hippos.

reigns.tagline: Noisy hippos, a war, and a king struck down
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by blows to the head
reigns.previously: Hyksos kings rule the north from Avaris; Thebes holds the south.
paragraphs: The story goes like this. Apepi, king at Avaris, sends a messenger all the way south to Thebes with a complaint: the hippos in Seqenenre's pool are making so much noise that Apepi can't sleep. Avaris is hundreds of miles away. It's an insult dressed up as an order, and Seqenenre and his court are left speechless. Then the papyrus breaks off, just as it's getting good.

The tale was written down long after, but it seems to remember a real clash, because Seqenenre's own body shows how he died. His mummy, found in the royal cache at Deir el-Bahri that came to light in 1881, has terrible head wounds from an axe, a spear or dagger, and a club. He was about 40. Some of the wounds match the shape of axes used by the Hyksos.

Did he fall in battle, or die some other way? A 2021 CT study by Sahar Saleem and Zahi Hawass argued that his hands had been tied, and that he was captured and executed on the battlefield. Not everyone agrees. Either way, Thebes was now at war with Avaris, and the fight passed to the next king, Kamose.

claims.text: Apepi picked a quarrel by complaining that Theban hippos were keeping him awake.
claims.note: From 'The Quarrel of Apophis and Seqenenre', a tale on a papyrus written centuries later. It breaks off before the end.

claims.text: Seqenenre was captured and executed on the battlefield.
claims.note: The 2021 CT study by Saleem and Hawass reads his hands as bound. Others think he simply died fighting, or was attacked in his sleep.

claims.text: He was killed by Hyksos weapons.
claims.note: Some wounds match Hyksos-style axes, but Egyptian and foreign weapons of the time were not always so different.

reigns.hook: Seqenenre is dead, killed by enemy blows. Kamose takes the throne at Thebes, and his advisers beg him to keep the peace.

reigns.tagline: He refused to share Egypt, and caught a spy to prove it
reigns.previously: Seqenenre Tao dies of terrible head wounds, probably in battle.
paragraphs: Kamose told his own story on two stelae at Karnak, and it starts with a grumble. What use is being king, he asks, when he sits wedged between a foreigner at Avaris and a Nubian in Kush, each holding a slice of Egypt? His councillors told him to stay put. Things were fine as they were, they said, and the Hyksos weren't troubling Thebes. Kamose wouldn't hear it.

He sailed north with his army, wrecking towns that had sided with the Hyksos, and came right up to Avaris. On the way his men caught a messenger on a desert road, carrying a letter from Apepi to the new ruler of Kush. It urged the Nubian to attack while Kamose was busy in the north, so they could crush him between them and share out Egypt. Kamose sent the messenger back to Apepi.

Then, after only a few years as king, Kamose died. How, nobody knows. His painted wooden coffin was found at Dra Abu el-Naga in 1857, but the mummy inside is said to have fallen to pieces. The war was not over. It passed to Seqenenre's son Ahmose, still a boy.

claims.text: Kamose fought his way to the walls of Avaris.
claims.note: His stela boasts of it, but he plainly didn't take the city, and how far he really got is hard to judge.

claims.text: His mummy crumbled to pieces soon after the coffin was found.
claims.note: That is the usual account of the 1857 find, but records of it are thin.

claims.text: Kamose was Seqenenre's son.
claims.note: Some make him Seqenenre's brother, or Ahmose's elder brother. No text spells out how they were related.

reigns.hook: Kamose is dead and the Hyksos still hold Avaris. The throne passes to Ahmose, a boy king with a formidable mother and a war to finish.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who drove out the Hyksos
reigns.previously: Kamose strikes north but dies with Avaris still untaken.
paragraphs: Ahmose was young when he became king, and in the early years others held things together. A stela at Karnak praises his mother, Queen Ahhotep, for caring for Egypt's soldiers, bringing back deserters and calming the south. Once Ahmose was grown, he went north to finish the war his father and Kamose had started. This is the founding of the 18th Dynasty and the start of the New Kingdom.

We know the campaign through an ordinary soldier. Ahmose son of Ebana, a fighting man from Elkab, had his life story carved in his tomb, and he keeps count of his rewards: gold for bravery, captives as slaves, and the hands he cut off dead enemies to prove each kill. He was there when Avaris fell. Then the army chased the Hyksos into southern Canaan and laid siege to Sharuhen for three years until it fell.

Ahmose turned south to Nubia too, and by the end of his reign, about 25 years later, Egypt was whole and on the road to empire. A strange stela from his time describes a terrible storm with rain and darkness. His queen, Ahmose-Nefertari, outlived him and was later worshipped as a goddess. Their son Amenhotep took the throne.

claims.text: Queen Ahhotep led Egypt's troops herself.
claims.note: The Karnak stela praises her for looking after the army and calming rebels. Gold flies, a military award, were found in a queen Ahhotep's burial, but there were two queens of that name and it's unclear whose it was.

claims.text: The storm on the Tempest Stela was the fallout of the volcanic eruption of Thera.
claims.note: An exciting idea, but the eruption's date is uncertain and the stela may describe a local storm, or use storm imagery for chaos.

claims.text: Ahmose son of Ebana fought at the fall of Avaris and the siege of Sharuhen.
claims.note: His tomb autobiography at Elkab tells it in his own words, listing every reward he won.

reigns.hook: Ahmose is gone and Egypt is whole. His son Amenhotep I inherits a quiet kingdom, and the workmen of Thebes are about to make him a saint.

reigns.tagline: The quiet king the tomb-builders turned into a god
reigns.previously: Ahmose has thrown out the Hyksos. Egypt is whole again and rising.
paragraphs: After his father's wars, Amenhotep I got something rare: about 20 fairly calm years. He was the son of Ahmose and Queen Ahmose-Nefertari, and his mother stayed a power at court for much of his reign. He built at Karnak, sent troops up the Nile into Nubia and kept the new state running. The records of his deeds are thin. His real legacy lay in one small village.

That was Deir el-Medina, home of the men who cut and painted the royal tombs at Thebes. Amenhotep and his mother became its patron saints, worshipped there for centuries after their deaths. When villagers fell out over a donkey, a debt or a stolen pot, they took the case to the deified king. Priests carried his statue out, and it gave its verdict by moving.

His mummy was rewrapped by priests about 3,000 years ago and has never been unwrapped since. In 2021 Sahar Saleem and Zahi Hawass unwrapped it digitally, with a CT scanner, without touching a bandage. Amenhotep left no surviving son. The crown passed to Thutmose, a tough army man.

claims.text: Amenhotep I founded the tomb-builders' village at Deir el-Medina.
claims.note: The villagers honoured him as their founder, but the oldest bricks there stamped with a king's name belong to Thutmose I.

claims.text: The deified king settled villagers' disputes as an oracle.
claims.note: Ostraca from Deir el-Medina record questions put to his statue and the answers it gave, for centuries after his death.

claims.text: The CT scan showed he died at about 35, with no sign of a violent death.
claims.note: Saleem and Hawass, Frontiers in Medicine, 2021. The age is an estimate from his bones and teeth.

reigns.hook: Amenhotep dies without a son. The new king, Thutmose, is a career soldier, and he wants to find out just how far Egypt's chariots can go.

reigns.tagline: The soldier king who planted a stone by the Euphrates
reigns.previously: Amenhotep I dies with no son. A soldier, Thutmose, takes the throne.
paragraphs: Thutmose I was probably not born into the main royal line. He seems to have been an army man, and once crowned he went looking for a fight. He sailed far up the Nile and smashed the kingdom of Kush. The soldier Ahmose son of Ebana, who was there, says the king came home with a Nubian chief hanging head-down from the prow of his ship.

Then he turned north-east. He marched through Canaan and Syria all the way to the Euphrates, a river that seemed to run backwards to Egyptian eyes, flowing south instead of north. On its bank he set up a stela to mark the edge of his world. Two generations later his grandson Thutmose III found it and set his own beside it.

He was probably the first king buried in the Valley of the Kings. His official Ineni dug the tomb and bragged that it was done with no one seeing and no one hearing. With his chief queen, Ahmose, he had a daughter, Hatshepsut. With a lesser wife, Mutnofret, he had a son, Thutmose II, who took the throne and married his half-sister.

claims.text: He sailed home with a Nubian chief hanging from the prow of his ship.
claims.note: Only Ahmose son of Ebana tells it, in his tomb autobiography at Elkab. An eyewitness, but a soldier who liked a boast.

claims.text: Thutmose I was the first king buried in the Valley of the Kings.
claims.note: Which tomb Ineni dug is still argued over, and the king's body was moved at least once in antiquity.

claims.text: He set up a stela on the bank of the Euphrates.
claims.note: Thutmose III's Annals at Karnak say he placed his own stela beside his grandfather's. Neither stone has been found.

reigns.hook: Thutmose II takes the throne, but he won't last long. Beside him stands his wife and half-sister, Hatshepsut, and she has plans of her own.

reigns.tagline: The queen who made herself king, false beard and all
reigns.reignEnded: Died; her images smashed years later
reigns.previously: Thutmose II dies young. His heir is a small boy, Thutmose III.
paragraphs: In 1479 BC her husband and half-brother Thutmose II died young. The heir was his small son by a lesser wife, Iset. The boy was crowned as Thutmose III, and Hatshepsut ran Egypt as his regent. Around 1473 BC she went further and had herself crowned king. The boy stayed king all along, and his reign is counted from 1479 BC, but for the next 15 years she was the senior king.

A woman king needed a story, and she carved one. Reliefs in her temple show the god Amun visiting her mother and fathering her. Her statues show her as a male king, false beard and all. Her temple, Djeser-djeseru, rises in terraces against the cliffs of Deir el-Bahri. Its walls show her fleet sailing to Punt and coming home with incense trees in pots, watched by Punt's very stout queen.

She raised two obelisks at Karnak, and one still stands. Her steward Senenmut, tutor to her daughter Neferure, rose from nowhere to huge power. When she died around 1458 BC, Thutmose III took over. About 20 years later her statues were smashed and her name chiselled off, probably to clear the way for his son Amenhotep II.

claims.text: Senenmut was Hatshepsut's lover.
claims.note: It rests mostly on a crude graffito in a quarry tomb near Deir el-Bahri. Nobody knows who drew it or whom it shows.

claims.text: Thutmose III wiped out her memory out of hatred.
claims.note: The attacks began some 20 years after her death, late in his reign. Securing his son's succession fits better than revenge.

claims.text: Her mummy was identified in 2007 by a single tooth.
claims.note: A molar in a box bearing her name matched a gap in a mummy from tomb KV60. Not every expert is convinced.

reigns.hook: Hatshepsut is dead, and the king she pushed aside is now a grown man. Thutmose III is about to make up for lost time, at the head of an army.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who waited 20 years, then conquered
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Thutmose II and Iset
reigns.previously: Hatshepsut dies after some 20 years as the senior king.
paragraphs: Thutmose III had been king since 1479 BC, when he was a small child, and his years are counted from then. Only in 1458 BC did he rule alone. He wasted no time. In 1457 BC Canaanite princes led by the king of Kadesh gathered at Megiddo. His generals begged him to take a safe road. He chose the narrow Aruna pass instead, marched the army through in single file and burst out to surprise the enemy.

The enemy fled inside Megiddo, and he besieged it for seven months until it gave in. That was the first of about 17 campaigns in Canaan and Syria, written up in his Annals at Karnak. He even had boats carried overland to cross the Euphrates. At Karnak he carved the strange plants and animals he had seen abroad, a stone botanical garden. James Henry Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt.

Two of his obelisks from Heliopolis now stand in London and New York, both nicknamed Cleopatra's Needle. Late in life he made his son Amenhotep II co-ruler, and around then Hatshepsut's name was hacked off her monuments. He died around 1425 BC, 54 years after he was first crowned.

claims.text: He beat the enemy at Megiddo by marching through the Aruna pass against his generals' advice.
claims.note: The story comes from his own Annals at Karnak, drawn from a war diary. The heroic framing is the king's.

claims.text: His general Djehuty took Joppa by smuggling soldiers into the city in baskets.
claims.note: Told in Papyrus Harris 500, written down long after. Djehuty was real, but the tale reads like Ali Baba.

claims.text: He crossed the Euphrates with boats dragged overland from the coast.
claims.note: His own inscriptions, including a stela at Gebel Barkal, say so. The details can't be checked.

reigns.hook: The great conqueror dies. His son Amenhotep II takes over, a strapping athlete who wants everyone to know just how strong he is.

reigns.title: Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV
reigns.tagline: A strongman show-off and a prince who dreamt of the Sphinx
reigns.previously: Thutmose III dies after 54 years as king, Egypt's greatest conqueror.
paragraphs: Amenhotep II had already shared the throne with his father for a couple of years (Shaw dates his reign from 1427 BC). Alone at last, he wanted the world to know how strong he was. His stelae claim he rowed harder than 200 sailors and shot arrows clean through thick copper targets from a speeding chariot. From Syria he brought home seven captured princes, hung upside-down from his ship.

His Amada stela says six of them were hanged on the walls of Thebes, and the seventh on the walls of Napata in Nubia, as a warning. His son Thutmose IV (1400 to 1390 BC) was gentler. Between the paws of the Great Sphinx stands his Dream Stela. As a prince, it says, he dozed off in the Sphinx's shade while out hunting. The god spoke to him: clear away the sand that buries me, and you will be king.

He cleared the sand and got the crown. Abroad, he made peace with Egypt's old enemy Mitanni in Syria and sealed it by marrying a Mitannian princess. He died young, around 1390 BC, and passed a rich and peaceful Egypt to his son, Amenhotep III.

claims.text: The Sphinx promised a sleeping prince the throne if he cleared away the sand.
claims.note: Carved after he became king. It looks like a younger son justifying his claim, and the end of the text is broken.

claims.text: Amenhotep II out-rowed 200 sailors and shot through copper targets.
claims.note: From his own stelae at Giza and elsewhere. Boasting about strength was part of a king's job.

claims.text: He hung captured Syrian princes upside-down on his ship.
claims.note: The Amada stela says so. It is royal propaganda, but cruelty to enemies was a normal royal boast.

reigns.hook: Thutmose IV is dead. His son Amenhotep III inherits Egypt at the peak of its wealth, and he means to spend it.

reigns.tagline: Egypt's richest king, and he wanted everyone to know
reigns.previously: Thutmose IV gets the crown he dreamt of, then dies young.
paragraphs: Amenhotep III ruled for about 38 years at the high noon of Egyptian wealth. His chief queen, Tiye, was not royal. Her parents, Yuya and Thuya, were a non-royal couple whose almost untouched tomb turned up in the Valley of the Kings in 1905. He announced the marriage on big carved scarabs sent out across the country, a kind of royal press release.

Other scarabs bragged of a wild bull hunt, a pleasure lake dug for Tiye, and 102 lions killed in his first ten years. He built Luxor temple and a vast temple on the west bank, whose giant guardians, the Colossi of Memnon, still sit there. In the Amarna letters he took Babylonian and Mitannian princesses as wives, but would not send a daughter abroad. No Egyptian king's daughter, he said, had ever been given away.

As he aged, the king of Mitanni sent him a statue of the goddess Ishtar, perhaps to heal him. Hundreds of statues of Sekhmet, the lioness goddess of plague and healing, may have had a similar job. He died around 1352 BC, and his son Amenhotep took the throne with some very new ideas.

claims.text: Amenhotep III refused to send a daughter abroad, saying no Egyptian king's daughter ever had been.
claims.note: Quoted back at him, with some irritation, by the Babylonian king in Amarna letter EA 4.

claims.text: One of the Colossi of Memnon 'sang' at dawn, and Roman tourists came to hear it.
claims.note: Greek and Latin graffiti on its legs record the sound after an earthquake cracked it. It fell silent after later repairs.

claims.text: The Mitannian king sent the statue of Ishtar to cure him.
claims.note: The letter (EA 23) says the goddess was sent to Egypt. It doesn't spell out why, so the healing idea is a guess.

reigns.hook: The old king is dead. His son Amenhotep IV seems ordinary at first. Within a few years he will change his name, shut the temples and build a new city in the desert.

reigns.title: Akhenaten & Nefertiti
reigns.tagline: The king who threw out the gods, and his famous queen
reigns.previously: Amenhotep III dies after nearly 40 glittering years.
paragraphs: He began as Amenhotep IV. Around his fifth year he became Akhenaten, devoted to the Aten, the sun disc whose rays end in little hands. Then came revolution. The old gods' temples were closed and Amun's name was hacked off monuments across Egypt. The court packed up and moved to a brand-new city, Akhetaten, built on empty desert. We call it Amarna.

Art changed too. The king appears with a long face and swollen belly, kissing and cuddling his six daughters. Always at his side was his queen, Nefertiti, worshipping beside him and even shown smiting enemies like a king. The Great Hymn to the Aten praises the sun as the maker of all life. Meanwhile Amarna letters from Canaanite vassals begged for troops that never came.

Nefertiti's painted bust was found at Amarna on 6 December 1912 by Ludwig Borchardt's team, in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose. It is in Berlin, and Egypt wants it back. She was long thought to vanish around year 12, but an inscription found in 2012 names her as queen in year 16. Akhenaten died around 1336 BC, and his revolution was left without a leader.

claims.text: Nefertiti ruled after Akhenaten as the female king Neferneferuaten.
claims.note: A woman did rule briefly under that name. Some Egyptologists think it was Nefertiti, others a daughter such as Meritaten.

claims.text: The strange art shows that Akhenaten had a disease.
claims.note: Ideas range from Marfan syndrome to hormone disorders. A 2010 DNA study found no sign, and the style may be religious.

claims.text: The Great Hymn to the Aten inspired Psalm 104.
claims.note: The likeness of theme and imagery is striking. Whether one text borrowed from the other can't be proved.

reigns.hook: After Akhenaten comes a blur of short reigns. Out of it steps a boy of about eight called Tutankhaten, and the old gods are waiting to come back.

reigns.tagline: The forgotten boy king who became the most famous of all
reigns.previously: Akhenaten dies. Short, murky reigns follow at Amarna.
paragraphs: He was born Tutankhaten, 'living image of the Aten', around 1345 BC, probably Akhenaten's son. Crowned at about eight or nine, he married his half-sister Ankhesenpaaten. Soon both changed names, to Tutankhamun and Ankhesenamun. His Restoration Stela promised to reopen the old temples, and the court turned back to the old gods. Real power lay with the courtier Ay and the general Horemheb.

He died at about 18 or 19, around 1327 BC, and nobody knows why. A 2010 study found a broken leg, a deformed foot and traces of malaria. The old idea that he was murdered with a blow to the head is now rejected. A royal widow then wrote to the Hittite king Suppiluliuma, begging for one of his sons as a husband. He sent a prince, Zannanza, who died on the way.

Then the boy was forgotten, and so was his small tomb. On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter's team, paid for by Lord Carnarvon, found its first step. The burial chamber was opened on 16 February 1923. Inside a nest of gilded shrines and coffins, reached only in 1925, lay the king in a solid gold mask. Carnarvon died that April, and the papers had their curse.

claims.text: Asked if he could see anything, Carter replied: 'Yes, wonderful things.'
claims.note: That is the line in his published book. His own notes and others present give slightly different words.

claims.text: The widow who begged the Hittites for a husband was Tutankhamun's wife, Ankhesenamun.
claims.note: The Hittite text calls her only Dahamunzu, 'the king's wife'. Some argue for Nefertiti or Meritaten.

claims.text: A curse killed Lord Carnarvon and others who opened the tomb.
claims.note: Carnarvon died of an infection, and Carter lived until 1939. The curse was a newspaper sensation.

reigns.tagline: The general who cleaned house and erased the heretics
reigns.previously: Old Ay takes the throne after Tutankhamun and reigns about four years.
paragraphs: Horemheb had commanded the army under Tutankhamun. When the old courtier Ay died, around 1323 BC, Horemheb took the throne himself. He set out to fix a country he thought had gone rotten. His Great Edict went after corrupt officials and tax men who robbed the poor. The guilty would have their noses cut off and be sent into exile at Tjaru, a fortress on the desert frontier.

Then he went after the memory of Akhenaten. He pulled down the Aten temples and packed their blocks inside the pylons of Karnak as rubble. Later king lists jump straight from Amenhotep III to Horemheb, as if Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ay had never been. The hidden blocks survived, though, and now help Egyptologists piece the Amarna story back together.

As a general he had built himself a splendid tomb at Saqqara, rediscovered in 1975. As king he had a new one dug in the Valley of the Kings. He had no surviving son, so he named his vizier and general Paramessu as heir, an old soldier who would rule as Ramesses I.

claims.text: His Great Edict punished corrupt officials by cutting off their noses.
claims.note: Carved on a broken stela at Karnak. How strictly it was enforced, nobody knows.

claims.text: Horemheb was the real power behind the boy king Tutankhamun.
claims.note: His Saqqara tomb gives him grand titles as the king's deputy, but he shared influence with Ay.

claims.text: Later Egyptians erased the Amarna kings from their king lists.
claims.note: The Abydos king list of Seti I goes straight from Amenhotep III to Horemheb.

reigns.hook: Horemheb hands Egypt to an old comrade. Ramesses I barely lasts a year, but his son Seti is ready, and he means to win the empire back.

reigns.previously: Horemheb's heir, the old soldier Ramesses I, reigns barely a year.
paragraphs: Ramesses I was already old when he took Horemheb's throne, and he reigned only about a year (1295 to 1294 BC). His son Seti inherited a new dynasty with no royal blood and something to prove. His name honours Seth, god of storms and chaos. He marched into Canaan and Syria to rebuild Egypt's empire, fought the Libyans and the Hittites, and for a time held the city of Kadesh.

At Abydos he built a beautiful temple with a famous list of 76 kings, showing him and his young son Ramesses honouring their ancestors. It quietly leaves out Hatshepsut and the Amarna kings. At Karnak the great Hypostyle Hall rose under his name, a forest of 134 giant columns.

His tomb, KV17, is among the longest and finest in the Valley of the Kings. Giovanni Belzoni found it in 1817, its paint still bright. His alabaster sarcophagus ended up in Sir John Soane's Museum in London. His mummy, found in the royal cache of 1881, still has a calm, handsome face. He had trained his son Ramesses well.

claims.text: Seti began the great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak.
claims.note: Some credit Horemheb or Ramesses I with the start. Seti decorated much of it and Ramesses II finished it.

claims.text: Seti captured Kadesh.
claims.note: His Karnak battle reliefs show it, but the city was soon back in the Hittite camp.

claims.text: His is one of the best-preserved royal mummies.
claims.note: A common verdict, though ancient robbers broke the head from the body.

reigns.hook: Seti dies, and his son steps up. Ramesses II will rule for 66 years, fill Egypt with his face, and fight the most famous battle of the age.

reigns.tagline: The king who fought a draw and carved it as a triumph
reigns.previously: Seti I dies, having restored Egypt's armies and its pride.
paragraphs: Ramesses II reigned for 66 years and made sure nobody would forget it. In 1274 BC, his fifth year, he marched on Kadesh in Syria against the Hittite king Muwatalli II. Two planted spies fed him a lie, and the Hittite chariots caught his army strung out on the march. Ramesses says he saved the day almost single-handed. At best it was a draw, but he carved his victory on temple walls all over Egypt.

In his year 21, about 1259 BC, he made peace with the next Hittite king, Hattusili III. Both versions survive, the Egyptian on temple walls and the Hittite on clay tablets. Later he married a Hittite princess. He built everywhere: a new Delta capital, Pi-Ramesses, and the rock temples of Abu Simbel, which were cut up and moved uphill in 1964 to 1968 to escape the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

He had over a hundred children and outlived many of his heirs. His queen Nefertari lies in a gorgeously painted tomb in the Valley of the Queens. Shelley's 1818 poem 'Ozymandias' takes its name from the Greek form of his throne name. He died around 1213 BC, aged about 90, and his 13th son took the throne.

claims.text: Ramesses won the battle of Kadesh almost single-handed.
claims.note: His own poem and reliefs tell it. Kadesh stayed Hittite, and Hittite sources suggest a stalemate at best.

claims.text: His treaty with the Hittites is the earliest surviving peace treaty.
claims.note: Often called so, and copies survive from both sides. Older Mesopotamian treaties exist, so it depends on definitions.

claims.text: In 1976 his mummy was issued a passport to fly to Paris.
claims.note: The mummy really did go to Paris for treatment against fungus. The passport story is widely told but hard to pin down.

reigns.hook: After 66 years, Egypt has a new king for the first time in most people's lives. Merneptah is already old, and enemies are gathering in the west.

reigns.tagline: The old prince whose stela first names Israel
reigns.previously: Ramesses the Great dies at about 90, after 66 years on the throne.
paragraphs: Merneptah had waited a very long time. He was the 13th son of Ramesses II, and the brothers ahead of him had all died before their father. By the time he was crowned he was probably in his sixties. There was no time to relax. In his fifth year, Libyan tribes pushed into the western Delta, joined by some of the Sea Peoples, raiders from around the Mediterranean. Merneptah's army crushed them.

He celebrated on a tall granite stela, which Flinders Petrie found at Thebes in 1896. Near the end it lists enemies beaten in Canaan, and boasts that Israel is laid waste and its seed is gone. It is the earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible. He also shipped grain to the Hittites, his father's old enemies, when famine struck them.

He died around 1203 BC. His mummy turned up in 1898, among the royal bodies hidden in the tomb of Amenhotep II. Older writers made him the pharaoh of the Exodus, though nothing backs that up. After him, the family of Ramesses began to tear itself apart.

claims.text: The Merneptah Stela is the earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible.
claims.note: The name is written with the sign for a people, not a place. Now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

claims.text: He sent grain to keep the Hittites alive in a famine.
claims.note: A Karnak inscription mentions shipping grain to Hatti. How much, and how bad the famine was, is debated.

claims.text: Merneptah was the pharaoh of the Exodus.
claims.note: A popular guess in older books. No Egyptian source mentions an Exodus, and the stela puts Israel already in Canaan.

reigns.hook: Merneptah's heirs turn on each other. A rival king grabs the south, a boy king limps onto the throne, and a foreign chancellor pulls the strings.

reigns.title: Seti II, Siptah and Tausret
reigns.tagline: A rival king, a boy pharaoh, a fallen chancellor, a queen
reigns.previously: Merneptah dies an old man, his Libyan war won.
paragraphs: Merneptah's death set off a family feud. His son Seti II was the rightful heir, but a prince called Amenmesse held Thebes and the south for a few years, either before Seti or against him. Seti came out on top and had his rival's name chiselled off the walls. Then he died too, after only about six years.

The next king, Siptah, was a boy with a badly twisted foot. The man running things was the chancellor Bay, a foreigner by birth, who boasted that he had set the king on his father's throne. He got too big. In Siptah's year 5 a message reached the tomb-builders' village of Deir el-Medina: Pharaoh had killed the great enemy Bay.

Siptah died young soon after. Seti II's widow Tausret, who had stood behind the throne all along, now took the crown herself and ruled alone as king, about 1188 BC. It lasted about two years. Then she disappears from the record, and Egypt slides into a short, ugly civil war.

claims.text: Amenmesse ruled before Seti II, not as his rival.
claims.note: Shaw's scheme puts Amenmesse first, from 1203 to 1200 BC. Others think he rebelled in the south during Seti's reign. The monuments can be read both ways.

claims.text: Siptah had the chancellor Bay executed.
claims.note: A Deir el-Medina ostracon, published by Pierre Grandet in 2000, announces that Pharaoh has killed 'the great enemy Bay' in year 5.

claims.text: The Deir el-Medina foreman Paneb stole from tombs, beat people and seduced workmen's wives.
claims.note: All of it comes from a list of charges in Papyrus Salt 124, written by a rival, Amennakht. We never hear Paneb's side.

reigns.hook: Tausret is gone. A man named Sethnakht, of unknown family, fights his way to the throne and starts a new dynasty. His son will face an invasion from the sea.

reigns.tagline: He beat the Sea Peoples, then his own wife plotted murder
reigns.reignEnded: Throat cut in the Harem Conspiracy
reigns.previously: Tausret vanishes. Sethnakht grabs the throne in the chaos.
paragraphs: His father Sethnakht seized power in the chaos after Queen Tausret and held it for about two years. Ramesses III, first great king of the 20th Dynasty, modelled himself on Ramesses II, and he needed to. Libyans pushed into the Delta twice and were thrown back. In his year 8 came the Sea Peoples, raiders and migrants who had wrecked cities across the eastern Mediterranean. He fought them on land and in the mouths of the Nile, and won.

His temple at Medinet Habu, on the west bank at Thebes, shows it all: ships locked together, enemies tumbling into the water, scribes counting heaps of hands and penises cut from the dead. But the money was running out. In year 29 the tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, their grain rations late, downed tools and marched on the temples to protest.

Then came the Harem Conspiracy. A lesser wife, Tiye, plotted to put her son Pentawer on the throne. The trial records survive: the guilty were sentenced to death or allowed to kill themselves, and some judges lost their noses and ears for partying with accused women. In 2012 a CT scan found a deep cut across the king's throat. The plotters probably got him, but not the crown. His son became Ramesses IV.

claims.text: The harem plotters succeeded in killing Ramesses III.
claims.note: A 2012 CT study by Zahi Hawass, Sahar Saleem and colleagues found a deep throat wound. The trial papers never say outright that the king died in the attack.

claims.text: 'Unknown Man E', a mummy wrapped in a goatskin, is Prince Pentawer.
claims.note: The same 2012 study found DNA showing a father-son link with Ramesses III. That fits Pentawer but cannot prove it.

claims.text: The Deir el-Medina walkout is the earliest strike on record.
claims.note: The Turin Strike Papyrus describes it day by day. 'Earliest' only means the earliest we know of.

reigns.hook: Ramesses III is dead and his son takes the throne. Eight more kings called Ramesses will follow, and each will rule over a little less than the one before.

reigns.title: The Last Ramessides
reigns.tagline: Eight kings called Ramesses, and a kingdom running down
reigns.reignEnded: Ramesses XI dies; New Kingdom ends
reigns.previously: Ramesses III dies, probably murdered by harem plotters.
paragraphs: Eight more kings called Ramesses, numbers IV to XI, reigned in about 84 years. None of them lived up to the name. Grain prices soared, Libyan raiders roamed Upper Egypt, and real power in the south drained away to the high priests of Amun at Karnak.

Under Ramesses IX officials investigated a wave of robberies in the royal tombs at Thebes. The robbers' confessions survive. They had tunnelled into the pyramid of Sobekemsaf, a 17th Dynasty king, found him lying beside his queen, and stripped both mummies of their gold. The inquiry soon turned into a feud between the mayors of east and west Thebes.

Late in Ramesses XI's reign, the high priest Herihor carved royal titles for himself in the temple of Khonsu at Karnak. The Story of Wenamun tells of an envoy sent to Byblos to buy cedar who is robbed on the way and sneered at by a local prince who no longer fears Egypt. When Ramesses XI died, the New Kingdom died with him.

claims.text: Robbers confessed to stripping the mummy of King Sobekemsaf.
claims.note: The Abbott and Leopold-Amherst papyri record the investigation and the thieves' own words under questioning.

claims.text: The Story of Wenamun is a real envoy's report.
claims.note: It reads like an official account, but many scholars treat it as literature that plays on Egypt's fallen prestige.

claims.text: Herihor took royal titles while Ramesses XI was still alive.
claims.note: Reliefs in the temple of Khonsu at Karnak give him a king's cartouche. How far he really claimed to be king is debated.

reigns.hook: Ramesses XI is dead. In the north a man called Smendes rules from the Delta. In the south the high priests of Amun answer to nobody but their god.

reigns.title: Kings at Tanis
reigns.tagline: Two Egypts, a hidden cache of kings, and a silver coffin
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Heirs to Ramesses XI's split realm
reigns.reignEnded: The Libyan chief Shoshenq takes over
reigns.previously: Ramesses XI dies. The New Kingdom is over.
paragraphs: Welcome to the Third Intermediate Period. Smendes, first king of the 21st Dynasty, ruled the north from Tanis in the Delta, while the high priests of Amun ran the south from Thebes. The two families married into each other, so Egypt was split without being at war. Tanis was built in a hurry from statues and stone blocks dragged over from Pi-Ramesses, Ramesses II's old capital.

At Thebes the priests faced an embarrassment: the royal tombs had been robbed. So they gathered up the great kings, Seti I, Ramesses II, Thutmose III and many more, rewrapped them and hid them in secret caches. One, at Deir el-Bahri, was found by the Abd el-Rassul family, who quietly sold its treasures for years until the authorities caught on in 1881.

In 1939 and 1940 Pierre Montet opened the royal tombs at Tanis. Psusennes I's burial was untouched: a silver coffin, a gold mask and piles of jewellery. With war breaking out, hardly anyone noticed. Meanwhile the dynasty faded, and in the Delta the Libyan army chiefs grew strong.

claims.text: A pharaoh of this time gave his daughter in marriage to King Solomon.
claims.note: Only the Bible (1 Kings) says so, and it never names the pharaoh. Siamun is the usual guess. Egyptian records are silent.

claims.text: The kings at Tanis and the priests at Thebes got on well.
claims.note: They intermarried and the priests dated documents by the Tanis kings' years, but how friendly they really were is unclear.

claims.text: Montet's finds were overshadowed by the Second World War.
claims.note: The tombs were opened in 1939 and 1940, and Tanis has never been as famous as Tutankhamun. How much the war was to blame is a judgement call.

reigns.hook: The last Tanis king dies. Waiting in the wings is Shoshenq, a great chief of the Libyans, whose family has lived in Egypt for generations.
