reigns.tagline: The Libyan chief who may have looted Solomon's temple
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Libyan army chief, no son of the last
reigns.previously: The Tanis kings fade. Libyan chiefs hold the real power.
paragraphs: Shoshenq came from a family of Libyan chiefs, the Meshwesh, settled at Bubastis in the Delta for generations. They were soldiers, Egyptian in religion but proud of their roots. As commander of the army he took the throne and founded the 22nd Dynasty. To bring Thebes into line, he made his son Iuput high priest of Amun.

Then he went to war. He marched into Canaan and Israel and carved a long list of the towns he took on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak. A broken piece of his victory stela turned up at Megiddo. He's usually taken to be the biblical Shishak, who carried off the treasures of Solomon's temple in Jerusalem. Oddly, Jerusalem isn't on his surviving list.
He began a vast new court at Karnak to show off his victories, but the reliefs on the portal were never finished. He died after about 21 years, and his son Osorkon I took over a rich, united kingdom.

claims.text: Shoshenq is Shishak, who took Solomon's treasures in Rehoboam's fifth year.
claims.note: The names and timing fit, but Jerusalem is missing from the Karnak list as it survives. Some think the city paid him off.

claims.text: He was a nephew of the earlier king Osorkon the Elder.
claims.note: Pieced together from family trees and a later genealogy. Most accept it, but it rests on thin evidence.

claims.text: A fragment of his victory stela was found at Megiddo.
claims.note: Excavators found it in the 1920s. It proves his army really reached the town.

reigns.hook: Shoshenq leaves a strong kingdom to his son. Within a few generations, though, the family is fighting itself, and Egypt will have several kings at once.

reigns.title: Egypt in Pieces
reigns.tagline: Too many kings, and none of them strong enough
reigns.previously: Shoshenq I dies, leaving a rich, united kingdom.
paragraphs: Shoshenq's son Osorkon I showered the temples with silver and gold. After him the grip slipped. Under Takelot II civil war broke out at Thebes when the king's son, Prince Osorkon, tried to impose himself as high priest of Amun. His own chronicle, carved at Karnak, boasts of executing the rebels, but the city rose against him again and again.

By the 8th century BC there were kings at Tanis, Leontopolis, Hermopolis and Herakleopolis, while at Sais the chiefs of the West, led by Tefnakht, were building a power base. At Thebes the God's Wives of Amun, royal princesses who never married, ran the god's huge estate.

The kings at Tanis were buried in stone tombs inside the temple walls, Osorkon II and Shoshenq III among them, with gold and silver to match. Far to the south, beyond the cataracts, the kingdom of Kush was watching.

claims.text: Prince Osorkon fought a long civil war for control of Thebes.
claims.note: His own Chronicle, carved at Karnak, tells the story. It is his version, so the rebels come off badly.

claims.text: The 23rd Dynasty ruled from Leontopolis.
claims.note: That is Manetho's version. Many Egyptologists now think the 23rd Dynasty was really a line of kings based at Thebes.

claims.text: The God's Wives of Amun became the real power at Thebes.
claims.note: Their titles, estates and tomb-chapels at Medinet Habu show it. Later rulers placed their own daughters in the job.

reigns.hook: Tefnakht of Sais is swallowing the Delta. Upriver, frightened princes look south to a king of Kush named Piye, who believes he is Amun's chosen one.

reigns.tagline: He conquered Egypt, then fussed over the horses
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Kashta, king of Kush
reigns.previously: Egypt is split among rival kings. Tefnakht of Sais is rising.
paragraphs: Piye, also written Piankhi, was king of Kush, ruling from Napata below the fourth cataract in what is now Sudan. The Kushites had taken Egyptian religion to heart and worshipped Amun at Gebel Barkal, their holy mountain. The Greeks later called them Ethiopians. When Tefnakht of Sais pushed south, Piye sent his army north and then came himself. He counts as the first of the 25th Dynasty, the Kushite 'black pharaohs'.

His great granite stela from Gebel Barkal tells the tale. He stopped at Thebes for the festivals, besieged Hermopolis and stormed Memphis. When King Nimlot of Hermopolis gave up, Piye toured the stables and was more upset that the horses had gone hungry than by the revolt. The Delta kings came to submit, but only Nimlot was let into the palace. The others ate fish, which made them unclean.
Then Piye sailed home to Napata, loaded with treasure, and as far as we know he never came back. He was buried under a pyramid at el-Kurru, with his horses buried nearby.

claims.text: Piye's horses were buried standing up.
claims.note: The horse burials at el-Kurru are real, but whether the animals were placed upright is an old description, not certain.

claims.text: Piye never returned to Egypt after his campaign.
claims.note: No source shows him back in Egypt, but the record is thin. It may just be silence.

claims.text: Piye's campaign came about 728 BC.
claims.note: The stela dates it to his year 21. Turning that into a BC date depends on when his reign began.

reigns.hook: Piye has left the old kings in charge. In the Delta, Sais is stirring again. His brother Shabaqo will have to come north and finish the job.

reigns.title: Shabaqo and Shebitqo
reigns.tagline: Kushite kings of all Egypt, and the shadow of Assyria
reigns.previously: Piye goes home to Napata, leaving the local kings in place.
paragraphs: Shabaqo (or Shabaka), probably Piye's brother, did what Piye hadn't. He came north and stayed, ruling all of Egypt as well as Kush. The Delta's ruler at Sais, Bakenrenef, whom the Greeks called Bocchoris, was swept away. Manetho says Shabaqo captured him and burned him alive.

Shabaqo had an eye for the past. Finding an old religious text 'eaten by worms', he had it copied onto a stone slab so it would survive. Much later somebody used the slab as a millstone and ground away the middle. It's now the Shabaka Stone in the British Museum.

Next came Shebitqo, though some scholars now think he actually reigned first. Either way a new danger loomed: Assyria. In 701 BC an Egyptian and Kushite army marched into Judah to stop King Sennacherib, and met him at Eltekeh. Sennacherib says he won.

claims.text: Shabaqo burned Bakenrenef (Bocchoris) of Sais alive.
claims.note: Only Manetho says so, in quotations by later writers. No Egyptian record mentions it.

claims.text: Shabaqo reigned before Shebitqo.
claims.note: That is the traditional order and Shaw's. New readings of Assyrian and Egyptian texts since 2013 have led some to put Shebitqo first.

claims.text: The Assyrians won at Eltekeh in 701 BC.
claims.note: Our only account is Sennacherib's own annals, which never admit a setback.

reigns.hook: Shebitqo dies in 690 BC. The new king is Taharqa, a son of Piye, who will build like Ramesses and take on the most feared army in the world.

reigns.tagline: The Kushite builder-king who took on Assyria
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Kush, Egypt slipping away
reigns.previously: Shebitqo dies. Assyria is on the march in the Levant.
paragraphs: Taharqa was Piye's son and the greatest builder of the Kushite pharaohs, with grand works at Karnak, Kawa and Gebel Barkal. In his year 6 the Nile rose higher than anyone could remember, and his stela boasts that it brought rich harvests and killed off the rats and snakes. The Bible remembers him as 'Tirhakah king of Kush', marching out against Sennacherib.

But Assyria was coming. In 671 BC King Esarhaddon took Memphis. Taharqa escaped, wounded according to the Assyrians, but his wife and his son Ushankhuru were taken. Taharqa won Memphis back, only for Ashurbanipal's army to drive him south again in 667 or 666 BC.
He died in 664 BC and was buried at Nuri under the biggest pyramid ever built in Kush. His claim to Egypt passed to his heir Tanutamani, who meant to win it back.

claims.text: A small kneeling prisoner on Esarhaddon's victory stela from Sam'al is Taharqa's son Ushankhuru.
claims.note: The figure wears Kushite-style dress and the capture is recorded, but the stela does not name him.

claims.text: Taharqa marched against Sennacherib, as 2 Kings and Isaiah say.
claims.note: In 701 BC he was not yet king. The Bible may be naming him by his later title, or mixing up campaigns.

claims.text: His pyramid at Nuri is the largest in Kush.
claims.note: It is the biggest at Nuri and usually called the largest Kushite pyramid, though it was enlarged in stages.

reigns.hook: Taharqa is dead and Tanutamani sweeps north to take Egypt back. But at Sais a local prince named Psamtik has thrown in his lot with Assyria.

reigns.tagline: Assyria's puppet who quietly took back all of Egypt
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Necho I of Sais
reigns.previously: Taharqa dies in 664 BC, with Egypt slipping from Kush's grip.
paragraphs: Psamtik's father Necho I, lord of Sais, died in 664 BC, probably fighting Taharqa's heir Tanutamani, who swept back into Egypt. The Assyrians answered by sacking Thebes in 663 BC, a disaster so famous that the prophet Nahum held it up as a warning to Nineveh. Psamtik, set up by Assyria as a vassal king, kept his head down.

Then, while Assyria was busy elsewhere, he quietly became his own master. He hired Greek and Carian mercenaries. By 656 BC he controlled Thebes, where his daughter Nitocris was adopted as the next God's Wife of Amun, a peaceful way to take over the south. Egypt was one kingdom again, under the 26th Dynasty, and the Late Period had begun.

Herodotus loved him. In one tale he had two babies raised by a shepherd who never spoke a word to them, to find the world's oldest language. Their first word was 'bekos', Phrygian for bread. Meanwhile his artists copied the styles of the Old Kingdom, as if Egypt wanted its golden age back.

claims.text: An oracle told Psamtik help would come from 'bronze men' rising from the sea, who turned out to be armoured Greek pirates.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, two centuries later. The Greek mercenaries were real; the oracle is a story.

claims.text: Psamtik's language experiment proved the Phrygians were older than the Egyptians.
claims.note: Herodotus heard it from priests at Memphis and says the Greeks told sillier versions.

claims.text: He besieged the city of Ashdod for 29 years.
claims.note: Herodotus calls it the longest siege he knew of. Nothing else backs up the number.

reigns.hook: Psamtik dies after 54 years. His son Necho II looks north, where Assyria is crumbling and Babylon is rising, and decides Egypt should join in.

reigns.tagline: The pharaoh who sent sailors all the way round Africa
reigns.previously: Psamtik I dies after 54 years, leaving Egypt rich and free.
paragraphs: Necho inherited a strong Egypt in a dangerous neighbourhood. Assyria, the old overlord, was collapsing under attack from Babylon and the Medes. Necho decided a weak Assyria was safer than a strong Babylon, so he marched north to help it. In 609 BC King Josiah of Judah came out to block his path at Megiddo, and was killed there.

For a few years Necho ran Syria and Canaan, even picking Judah's next king. Then in 605 BC the Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar smashed his army at Carchemish on the Euphrates. Egypt's empire in Asia was gone almost overnight, and Necho fell back to guard his own frontier.

At home he thought big. He started digging a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea and built war galleys for both seas. Herodotus says he also hired Phoenician crews to sail right round Africa. Necho died in 595 BC, and his son Psamtik II took the throne.

claims.text: Phoenician sailors sent by Necho sailed round Africa in about three years, and saw the sun on their right as they went round the south.
claims.note: Only Herodotus tells it, and he didn't believe the sun detail. That detail is exactly what you would see south of the equator, which persuades many that the voyage really happened.

claims.text: Necho gave up his canal after 120,000 workers died and an oracle warned he was building it for a foreigner.
claims.note: Herodotus, writing about 150 years later. The 'foreigner' was taken to be Darius I, who did finish a canal there.

claims.text: Nebuchadnezzar crushed Necho's army at Carchemish in 605 BC.
claims.note: Recorded in the Babylonian Chronicle and echoed in the Bible (Jeremiah 46).

reigns.hook: Necho's son Psamtik II inherits a smaller empire, an army of Greek mercenaries, and a grudge against the Kushite kings who once ruled Egypt.

reigns.title: Psamtik II and Apries
reigns.tagline: Graffiti on Ramesses' legs, then a mutiny in the ranks
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son and grandson of Necho II
reigns.previously: Necho II dies. His empire in Asia is lost, but Egypt is still rich.
paragraphs: Psamtik II reigned only six years, but he made them count. In 593 BC he sent an army deep into Kush, homeland of the old 25th Dynasty. On the way his Greek and Carian mercenaries stopped at Abu Simbel and scratched their names into the legs of Ramesses II's giant statues. Back home he had the names of the Kushite pharaohs hacked off monuments.

His son Apries, the Hophra of the Bible, took over in 589 BC and tried to make trouble for Babylon. He egged on Judah to revolt, which ended in disaster: Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Then in 570 BC Apries sent an army against Cyrene, the Greek city in Libya. It was beaten, and the survivors decided the king had sent them off to die.

The troops mutinied. Apries sent his general Amasis to talk them round, and the soldiers made Amasis king instead. Apries fought back with his Greek mercenaries and lost. A few years later he was dead.

claims.text: Greek and Carian soldiers carved their names on the colossi of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel.
claims.note: The graffiti are still there, among the oldest Greek inscriptions known. One names the expedition's leaders under 'King Psammetichos'.

claims.text: When Apries's envoy Patarbemis came back without Amasis, Apries had his nose and ears cut off, and the outraged Egyptians went over to Amasis.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 2. A good story told over a century later, with no Egyptian evidence.

claims.text: Apries was killed around 567 BC while trying to win back his throne.
claims.note: A damaged stela of Amasis seems to describe a battle and Apries's burial. Herodotus says the crowd strangled him. Dates and details differ.

reigns.hook: A general with a crude sense of humour is now king of Egypt. He will rule for over 40 years, charm the Greeks, and die just before the storm.

reigns.tagline: The joking, drinking general the Greeks adored
reigns.reignEnded: Died just before the Persians came
reigns.previously: Mutinous troops crown the general Amasis. Apries is finished.
paragraphs: The Greeks called him Amasis, and they loved him. He was a soldier of humble birth, and Herodotus fills pages with stories about him: a joker, a drinker, a man who never pretended to be grander than he was. When Apries summoned him during the mutiny, he is said to have answered by breaking wind and telling the messenger to take that back.

As king he was shrewd. He made Naukratis in the Delta the official base for Greek traders, sent rich gifts to Greek temples and made friends with Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos. He took Cyprus. Egypt had rarely been so peaceful or so rich.

But to the east, Persia was swallowing everything. Cyrus the Great took Lydia and then Babylon, and Egypt was clearly next on the list. Amasis died in 526 BC, months before the blow fell, leaving his son Psamtik III to face it.

claims.text: Amasis melted down a golden footbath and made it into a statue of a god, to show his subjects that something humble could become worthy of honour, just like him.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 2. A lovely parable, but nothing outside Herodotus backs it up.

claims.text: He worked in the mornings and drank in the afternoons, telling critics that a bow kept strung all the time will snap.
claims.note: Herodotus again, who loved Amasis stories. Treat it as character sketch, not history.

claims.text: Amasis broke off his friendship with Polycrates after Polycrates threw away a precious ring and got it back inside a fish.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 3. Amasis supposedly decided a man that lucky was doomed. Polycrates did come to a grisly end.

reigns.hook: Amasis is dead. His son Psamtik III has barely settled on the throne when the Persian king Cambyses arrives at the edge of the Delta with the army of the greatest empire on earth.

reigns.tagline: The Persian conqueror who put on the double crown
reigns.reignEnded: Died of a wound on the way home
reigns.previously: Amasis dies. His son Psamtik III inherits Persia at the door.
paragraphs: Cambyses, son of Cyrus the Great, came for Egypt in 525 BC. He met the new pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium, the gateway to the eastern Delta, and won. Memphis fell after a siege and Psamtik was taken prisoner. For the first time Egypt was a province of the Persian empire, and later king lists count Cambyses as the founder of the 27th Dynasty.

Egyptian records show him taking care to act the pharaoh. Udjahorresnet, who had commanded Egypt's navy, says on his statue that he gave Cambyses an Egyptian throne name and that the king cleared squatters out of the temple of Neith at Sais. Greek writers told a darker story, of a cruel madman who mocked Egypt's gods.

Herodotus adds an army lost in the desert and a failed march on Kush. In 522 BC news came of a rebellion back in Persia. Cambyses set off for home, but died on the way in Syria, from a wound in his thigh.

claims.text: Cambyses went mad and stabbed the sacred Apis bull, which died of the wound.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, but records from the Apis burial ground at Saqqara show a bull buried with full honours in Cambyses' reign.

claims.text: An army of 50,000 sent to the oasis of Siwa vanished in a sandstorm.
claims.note: Only Herodotus reports it. Explorers still hunt for the lost army, so far without convincing finds.

claims.text: At Pelusium the Persians drove cats and other sacred animals in front of their lines, so the Egyptians would not shoot.
claims.note: Told by the Greek writer Polyaenus some 700 years later. Herodotus, much closer in time, doesn't mention it.

reigns.hook: Cambyses is dead and Persia is in chaos. Out of it climbs Darius, a distant royal cousin, who will win over Egypt's priests by behaving like a true pharaoh.

reigns.tagline: The Persian who finished the pharaohs' canal
reigns.previously: Cambyses dies on the road home. Persia's throne is up for grabs.
paragraphs: Darius took the Persian throne in 522 BC by killing the man who held it, then spent a year crushing revolts across the empire. Egypt was one of the rebel provinces. Later, Herodotus says, Darius had his governor of Egypt, Aryandes, put to death for minting his own silver coins, a privilege that belonged to the king.

In Egypt, Darius played the pharaoh better than any Persian before or after. He sent Udjahorresnet home to restore the House of Life at Sais, a temple school for scribes and doctors. He built a temple to Amun at Hibis in the Kharga oasis, which still stands. Later Egyptians remembered him as a great lawgiver.

His proudest work was finishing Necho's canal from the Nile to the Red Sea. Along it he set up granite stelae in hieroglyphs and Persian cuneiform, boasting that ships now sailed from Egypt to Persia. After the Persian defeat at Marathon in 490 BC, Egypt rose in revolt again. Darius died in 486 BC before he could deal with it.

claims.text: Darius had Egypt's laws collected and written down.
claims.note: Reported by the Demotic Chronicle, written centuries later, and by Diodorus, who lists him among Egypt's great lawgivers.

claims.text: Aryandes was executed for striking his own silver coinage.
claims.note: Herodotus, book 4. Some historians think the real charge was rebellion, and the coins just a sign of it.

claims.text: A statue of Darius carved in Egypt, with hieroglyphs on its base, was found at Susa in Persia.
claims.note: Excavated at Susa in 1972 and now in Tehran. The base lists the peoples of the empire.

reigns.hook: Darius is dead and Egypt is in open revolt. His son Xerxes is coming, and he has none of his father's patience with Egyptian priests.

reigns.title: Under the Great King
reigns.tagline: Eighty years as a Persian province, and one big revolt
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Xerxes, son of Darius I, and heirs
reigns.previously: Darius dies with Egypt in revolt. Xerxes inherits the problem.
paragraphs: Xerxes crushed the Egyptian revolt in his second year and, Herodotus says, left the country far more firmly enslaved than before, with his own brother Achaemenes as governor. For the next eighty years Egypt was a province governed for the Great King, under Xerxes, Artaxerxes I and Darius II, all ruling from far-off Persia.

Around 460 BC a Libyan prince named Inaros rose up and called in Athens, which sent a fleet. Achaemenes was killed in battle. Then the Persian general Megabyzus struck back, trapped the Greeks on the island of Prosopitis in the Delta and destroyed the expedition. Inaros was captured and later put to death.

A few years later Herodotus came sightseeing, quizzing priests and guides; book 2 of his Histories is the result. Far south on Elephantine Island, Jewish soldiers in the Persian garrison left a pile of papyrus letters. In 410 BC priests of the local god Khnum destroyed their temple, and they wrote to the governor of Judah for help.

claims.text: Megabyzus besieged the Athenians on Prosopitis for 18 months, and almost none of them got home.
claims.note: Thucydides, book 1. He gives no total, and historians argue over how large the Athenian force and its losses really were.

claims.text: The Jews of Elephantine petitioned the governor of Judah to rebuild the temple the priests of Khnum had destroyed.
claims.note: Drafts of the petition, written in Aramaic in 407 BC, survive among the Elephantine papyri.

claims.text: Herodotus visited Egypt around the 440s BC.
claims.note: He clearly went, but never says when; the date is worked out from hints in his text.

reigns.hook: Darius II is dead, and in the Delta a prince of Sais named Amyrtaeus sees his chance to throw the Persians out.

reigns.title: Egypt Free Again
reigns.tagline: Persia's grip slips, and Egypt rules itself again
reigns.previously: Darius II dies in 404 BC, and Persia's hold on Egypt starts to slip.
paragraphs: Amyrtaeus of Sais led the break from Persia, and before long the Jewish soldiers on Elephantine were dating their papers by his reign instead of the Persian king's. He is the only king of the 28th Dynasty. Within a few years he was overthrown by Nepherites of Mendes, founder of the 29th, and a papyrus letter hints that Amyrtaeus was put to death at Memphis.

The new kings knew Persia would be back, so they went looking for friends. Nepherites I sent Sparta grain and gear for 100 warships. Hakor, whom the Greeks called Achoris, allied with King Evagoras of Cyprus and hired the Athenian general Chabrias. In the 380s BC a Persian attack on Egypt came to nothing.
At home the royal family squabbled over the throne. In 380 BC a general from Sebennytos named Nakhtnebef pushed aside the last king of the 29th Dynasty and took the crown for himself.

claims.text: Amyrtaeus was executed at Memphis by Nepherites.
claims.note: Based on one Aramaic letter from Elephantine. The wording is brief and its meaning is argued over.

claims.text: Nepherites I sent Sparta grain and equipment for 100 triremes.
claims.note: Diodorus, writing over 300 years later. It fits Egypt's need for allies, but no Egyptian source records it.

claims.text: Hakor hired the Athenian general Chabrias to command his forces.
claims.note: Diodorus and the Roman writer Cornelius Nepos. Athens later called Chabrias home under Persian pressure.

reigns.hook: Nakhtnebef, the Greeks' Nectanebo, has the throne. Now he has to keep it, because Persia is gathering a huge army to take Egypt back.

reigns.tagline: Saved by a quarrel and a flood, then built everywhere
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Took the throne from the 29th Dynasty
reigns.previously: The 29th Dynasty falls. A general from Sebennytos takes over.
paragraphs: Nakhtnebef, to the Greeks Nectanebo, was a soldier from Sebennytos in the Delta. He founded the 30th Dynasty, the last line of native kings. His big test came in 373 BC, when the Persian commander Pharnabazus landed in the Delta with a huge army, joined by the Athenian general Iphicrates and his Greek mercenaries.

It should have been the end. Iphicrates wanted to dash straight for Memphis before the Egyptians were ready, but Pharnabazus insisted on waiting for the whole army. The two men fell out, the Egyptians dug in, and then the Nile began to rise and flood the Delta. The invaders gave up and sailed away.

Safe again, Nectanebo built all over Egypt. He lined the road leading from Luxor temple with sphinxes, and some of the earliest buildings on the island of Philae are his. A stela at Naukratis gave the goddess Neith a tenth of the taxes on Greek trade. He died in 362 BC and his son Teos took over.

claims.text: The Persian invasion of 373 BC failed because the generals quarrelled and the Nile flood caught them.
claims.note: Diodorus, book 15, writing centuries later and from the Greek side. Egyptian sources say nothing about it.

claims.text: Nectanebo I put up the earliest buildings that survive on Philae.
claims.note: His gateway and kiosk are the oldest standing remains there, but earlier temples may have stood on the island.

claims.text: The Naukratis stela gave the temple of Neith at Sais a tenth of the taxes on Greek trade.
claims.note: The stela was found at Naukratis in 1899 and is in Cairo. A twin copy was later found underwater at Thonis-Heracleion.

reigns.hook: Nectanebo's son Teos has big plans: take the war to Persia. To pay for it, he is about to tax everything in Egypt that moves.

reigns.tagline: He hired Sparta's king to fight for him and lost his crown
reigns.previously: Nectanebo I dies after beating off Persia. His son Teos takes over.
paragraphs: Teos, Djedhor in Egyptian, decided to attack Persia instead of waiting to be attacked. Armies cost money, so he squeezed the temples and taxed whatever he could. Then he hired the best soldiers he could find. Agesilaus II, the aged king of Sparta, came to lead the Greek mercenaries, and the Athenian Chabrias took charge of the fleet.

The Egyptians were not impressed at first. They expected a mighty warrior and found a small old man in plain clothes. The two kings then argued over who was in charge. Teos marched into Persian Syria anyway, leaving his brother to run Egypt.

That was his mistake. Back home the brother had his own son Nectanebo, Teos's nephew, proclaimed king. Nectanebo was with the army in Syria, and Agesilaus came over to his side. Teos was left with nothing. He fled to his enemy, the Persian king, and seems to have died in exile.

claims.text: The Egyptians laughed at Agesilaus when they saw the famous Spartan king was a small, plainly dressed old man.
claims.note: Plutarch, Life of Agesilaus, written over 400 years later. Agesilaus was in his eighties and known for his simple ways.

claims.text: Teos raised his war chest by seizing temple wealth and taxing almost every sale.
claims.note: Described in the Greek Oeconomica, once credited to Aristotle. Its tips on raising cash may be exaggerated.

claims.text: Teos died in exile at the Persian court.
claims.note: Greek writers say he fled to Persia. When and how he died is not recorded.

reigns.hook: Nectanebo II has a crown, a Spartan king on his side and a rival claimant marching against him. He is often called the last native pharaoh of Egypt.

reigns.tagline: Egypt's last native pharaoh, or Alexander's secret father?
reigns.previously: Teos is abandoned by his army and flees to Persia. His nephew is king.
paragraphs: Nakhthorheb, the Greeks' Nectanebo II, had to fight for his crown at once. A rival claimant from Mendes raised an army against him, and Agesilaus helped beat him before sailing for home. Then the new Persian king, Artaxerxes III, invaded Egypt, and around 351 BC he was thrown back.

Nectanebo was devout and a busy builder, and temples all over Egypt carry his name. In 343 BC Artaxerxes came again with a far bigger army, and Greek mercenaries fought on both sides. Pelusium fell and the Persians pushed into the Delta. Nectanebo fled south and disappeared from history.

The Greeks wouldn't let him go so easily. A later romance made him a magician who escaped to Macedon and became the father of Alexander the Great. His empty stone sarcophagus turned up in Alexandria, where people came to believe it was Alexander's own. It is now in the British Museum.

claims.text: Nectanebo fled to Macedon, seduced Queen Olympias disguised as the god Ammon, and fathered Alexander the Great.
claims.note: From the Alexander Romance, a Greek fantasy written centuries later. It turned Egypt's last native king into Alexander's father.

claims.text: Nectanebo II was the last native Egyptian pharaoh.
claims.note: Commonly said, and he was the last to rule all of Egypt. Later rebels such as Khababash held parts of it for a while.

claims.text: After fleeing Memphis he went to Upper Egypt or on to Kush.
claims.note: Diodorus says he fled to 'Ethiopia', which may mean Kush. Some think he held out in the south for a while.

reigns.hook: Nectanebo is gone. Artaxerxes III owns Egypt again, and he means to make it pay for sixty years of freedom.

reigns.title: The Second Persian Period
reigns.tagline: Persia's revenge, then Alexander walks in
reigns.previously: Nectanebo II flees south. Persia owns Egypt once more.
paragraphs: Artaxerxes III took his revenge. Diodorus says he tore down city walls, looted the temples and carried off the sacred books, which his minister Bagoas later sold back to the priests for huge sums. Later writers went further and said the king killed the sacred Apis bull and had it cooked for a feast.

Bagoas, a eunuch, then poisoned Artaxerxes in 338 BC and his son Arses two years later. He put Darius III on the throne, and Darius made him drink his own poison. Meanwhile a native rebel named Khababash seems to have held parts of Egypt for a time, though nobody knows exactly when.

Then came Alexander of Macedon. After he beat Darius III at Issus in 333 BC, Egypt's Persian governor Mazaces had no army left. When Alexander reached Pelusium late in 332 BC, Mazaces handed the country over without a fight. Alexander went on to Memphis and sacrificed to the gods there, the Apis bull among them. Egypt's age of the pharaohs was giving way to the Greeks.

claims.text: Artaxerxes III killed the Apis bull and had it served up at a feast.
claims.note: Told by Aelian and other writers centuries later, perhaps modelled on the Cambyses story.

claims.text: The eunuch Bagoas poisoned both Artaxerxes III and his son Arses.
claims.note: Diodorus says so. Babylonian sources confirm the reigns, but not how they ended.

claims.text: Alexander was formally crowned pharaoh at Memphis.
claims.note: Only the Alexander Romance describes a coronation. Arrian, the best source, just says he sacrificed to Apis and held games.
